title: Sick with love (10:3, Song of Songs 2:5)
hookLine: love God like someone lovesick, who can't stop thinking of the beloved
tomorrow: but what if you're only in it for the extra credit?

lines: THE PHONE FACE-UP ON THE DESK.
A CRUSH IN A LAW BOOK?
cards: Somebody with a new crush can't concentrate on anything: the phone face-up on the desk, the name doodled in the margin of their notes, every song suddenly about one person. Here's the odd part.
That exact picture shows up in a book of Jewish law, describing how to love God. And to prove it, Maimonides quotes a love song from the Bible.

teach.b: What is the fitting love, he asks?
A love so great and strong that the soul is bound up in it, always absorbed in it, like someone lovesick, whose mind is never free of the one they love: sitting, standing, eating, drinking.
Even more than that, he says, should love of God fill the hearts of those who love Him. Then come the proofs.

teach.h: ALL YOUR HEART, ALL YOUR SOUL.
teach.b: Deuteronomy commands loving God with all your heart and all your soul.
And Solomon, Maimonides says, said it as a parable, in the Song of Songs: "for I am sick of love." He adds that the whole Song of Songs is a parable for this. So, the puzzle.

Why would a law book reach for a love song? Because a law can command an act, but this command is love, and love needs a picture. The clearest picture of a mind that keeps drifting back to someone is a person in love.
He isn't alone in reading the Song this way.
In the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva calls it the holy of holies among the writings.
One honest note: some modern readers take the Song first as human love poetry, two lovers among vineyards and apples. The tradition Maimonides draws on hears God and Israel inside it.
Here's the thing to tell a friend: in this law book, the measure of love isn't a feeling at prayer time. It's how often the mind comes back.

how: The Song of Songs is read in synagogue on Passover, and some Jews sing it on Friday afternoons before Shabbat; Maimonides' 10:3 is a classic text on loving God.

o: a weakness that comes from fasting and prayer
a love for God that keeps the mind coming back
a guilty feeling for loving the world too much

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: for I am sick of love
all your heart and all your soul
the Song is the holy of holies

s: a law book would never compare loving God to a crush
Maimonides does, in 10:3: like someone lovesick, never free of the beloved.
Maimonides says the whole Song of Songs is a parable for this love
he quotes 'for I am sick of love' as Solomon's parable.

games.q: a friend laughs: 'the Song of Songs is basically a steamy poem. why is that in the Bible?' how would Maimonides answer?
o: it's a parable for loving God: a mind bound up in love.
it shouldn't be there; the sages tried to remove it.
it's only a love poem; God has nothing to do with it.
games.why: Maimonides calls the whole Song a parable for loving God, and Akiva calls it the holy of holies. some modern readers take it first as human love poetry.

practice: Choose one sound you can hear right now: a fan, traffic, your own breath.

Let your attention rest on it, and when it wanders, notice that it wandered and bring it back, gently, the way a mind in love keeps drifting back to one name. Stay with that coming back until the bell.
